food.text: In November 2004, chefs and food professionals from all the Nordic countries met in Copenhagen to discuss what they called the 'New Nordic Cuisine'. They stressed 'purity, simplicity and freshness' and more use of seasonal foods. Restaurants were encouraged to build dishes around ingredients suited to the local region's climate, water and soil.

Arla Foods was formed on 17 April 2000, when the Swedish dairy co-operative Arla merged with the Danish dairy company MD Foods. The name Arla comes from an archaic Swedish term meaning 'early (in the morning)'. The company is a co-operative based in Viby, Denmark.

Lingonberry jam is a staple of Scandinavian cuisine, served with meatballs, beef stew, liver dishes and fried herring. It also accompanies traditional dishes such as kroppkakor, potato pancakes and black pudding. Thanks to the benzoic acid in lingonberries, the berries keep well without preservatives.

Copenhagen's Noma restaurant takes its name from nordisk mad, meaning 'Nordic food'. It served dishes prepared under the new cuisine's guidelines and was named 'world's best restaurant' by Restaurant magazine in 2010, 2011, 2012 and again in 2014.

On 26 April 1915, dairy farmers in Stockholm and adjoining counties created Sweden's largest co-operative dairy organisation, which ran dairies and a chain of shops selling dairy products. In 1927 it registered the name Mjölkcentralen, and in 1975 it changed its name to Arla.

When Iceland started commercial whaling, mostly of minke whales, in the early 20th century, whale meat became popular as a low-priced red meat. Iceland withdrew from the International Whaling Commission in 1992, and commercial whaling recommenced in 2006. Whale meat is commonly available again, though the price has gone up.

New influences have entered traditional Sámi cooking in recent decades. A well-known cross-cooked dish is the Suovaskebab, made of sliced suovasbierggo, cucumber, salad and garlic dressing in a pita bread. It can be found at festivals and fairs in northern Scandinavia, and some fast food restaurants in Sápmi serve reindeer hamburgers.

Meeting in Copenhagen in 2005, the Nordic Council's agricultural and food ministers from Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden backed the movement. They launched what they called the 'new Nordic Food Programme'. In 2006 this led to EUR 3 million of funding for related activities.

The Swedish chef Magnus Nilsson pioneered New Nordic Cuisine with an approach that includes documenting and reviving traditional cooking from across the Nordic region. His small restaurant Fäviken in rural Sweden closed in 2019 but was very influential in developing the cuisine.

To deal with the Great Depression in 1930, the Icelandic government instituted state monopolies on various imports, including vegetables. Regional farmers' cooperatives were granted a monopoly on dairy and meat production for the consumer market. This put smaller private producers out of business.

At the annual Food and Fun chef's competition, held in Iceland since 2004, competitors create innovative dishes with fresh ingredients produced in Iceland. Modern Icelandic chefs usually emphasise the quality of available ingredients rather than age-old cooking traditions and methods.

In March 2006, Arla took out full page advertising in Saudi Arabia, apologising for the cartoons and indicating Arla's respect for Islam in the country. This came during a two-month boycott of Danish products across the Middle East, which began over satirical cartoons of Prophet Muhammad published in Denmark and cost Arla US$2 million a day in lost sales. The advertisement caused controversy in Denmark, where women's organisations and some politicians criticised Arla and called on Danish women to boycott its products. In April 2006 the company said its products were being placed back in shops in the Middle East.

art.text: Tromsdalen Church, nicknamed the Arctic Cathedral, was built in 1965 to plans by architect Jan Inge Hovig. It is made of cast-in-place aluminium-coated concrete panels, and its shape is believed to echo the nearby twin-peaked island of Håja.

Scandinavian design emerged in the early 20th century as a movement built on simplicity, minimalism and functionality. It flourished in the 1950s across the five Nordic countries: Denmark, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and Iceland.

Danish design was influenced by the German Bauhaus school and combined new industrial technologies with simplicity and functionalism. Many of its pieces have become iconic, such as Arne Jacobsen's 1958 Egg chair and Poul Henningsen's 1926 PH-lamps.

Harry Haerendel's Der alte Seebär shows a bearded old sailor in a sou'wester smoking a pipe. Known in Scandinavia as Fiskargubben, its prints were very popular there in the mid to late 20th century and have been called a noted example of kitsch art.
In 1954, the Brooklyn Museum held its "Design in Scandinavia" exhibition. It kicked off a fashion for "Scandinavian Modern" furniture in America.
Design in Iceland is a young tradition that began in the 1950s. Limited manufacturing options and materials forced designers to be innovative, though wool remains a staple, whether felted or knitted.

Functionalist architecture emerged after World War I as part of Modernism, driven by a desire to build a better world for people. It reached Scandinavia and Finland from the 1930s, later than in Czechoslovakia, Germany, Poland, the USSR and the Netherlands.

In 1972 a glass mosaic titled "The Return of Christ" by Victor Sparre was added to the eastern side of the Arctic Cathedral. In 2005 the church acquired an organ from Grönlunds Orgelbyggeri, with 42 stops and 2940 pipes.
The Lunning Prize was awarded to outstanding Scandinavian designers between 1951 and 1970. It was instrumental in making Scandinavian design a recognized commodity and in defining its profile.

In 1914, the Danish Selskabet for Dekorativ Kunst launched a magazine called Skønvirkeda, meaning "Graceful Work". Its title became the name of a new Danish style of arts and crafts in objects and architecture, meant to rival Art Nouveau and Jugendstil.

Scandinavia House's galleries host exhibitions of Scandinavian painting, sculpture, photography and design. They have included solo shows of Nordic artists such as Edvard Munch and Vilhelm Hammershøi.

art.text: Iceland's Museum of Design and Applied Art opened in 1998, aiming to record Icelandic design from 1900 onwards. The Iceland Academy of the Arts was also founded in 1998, soon followed by its Faculty of Architecture and Design.
tags: Museum of Design and Applied Art

war.text: Germany invaded both Denmark and Norway on the same day, 9 April 1940. The attack came only days before Britain had planned to invade. Both sides had feared their enemies would gain power in Scandinavia.
German troops invaded Norway in 1940 with the Wehrmacht, and the German Army then occupied all of Norway until May 1945.

Norway, Denmark and Iceland became founding members of NATO in 1949 for defence against the Soviet Union and other potential invaders. Finland later joined NATO in 2023, and Sweden in 2024, in response to the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Germany valued the Swedish iron ore it received through Norway and could not afford to lose it. It also wanted Norway for its ice-free ports, making Norway the primary target. Denmark was a secondary goal, needed mainly to help the Norwegian invasion.

Near the start of World War II in late 1939, Britain believed Germany was planning to invade Scandinavia and made counter plans for its own invasion. Germany, meanwhile, feared Britain could gain bases in the area and claimed to suspect an outright invasion.

Finland allied with Nazi Germany and joined the German Army in invading the Soviet Union in spring 1941. Finland had a grievance because the Red Army had invaded southeastern Finland in the Winter War of 1939–40 and taken a large area of territory.

The Scandinavian defence union failed when Norway resigned from the talks after learning the western alliance could not supply the Scandinavian countries with armaments before meeting its own needs. Denmark was still willing to ally with Sweden, but the Swedes saw few advantages. Norway and Denmark then signed the North Atlantic Treaty.
Finland gained access to the Barents Sea in 1920, but the borders stayed fluid. In 1944 Finland ceded this territory to the Soviet Union.

literature.text: In 1956 Harry Martinson published Aniara, a poetic space epic. Martinson was known as one of Sweden's finest nature poets. In 1974 he shared the Nobel Prize in Literature with Eyvind Johnson.
The Nobel Prize in Literature is itself a Scandinavian award. Nordic winners include Sigrid Undset, Halldór Laxness, Eyvind Johnson, Harry Martinson, Tomas Tranströmer and Jon Fosse.

Tomas Tranströmer (1931–2015) is arguably the most famous Swedish poet of the 20th century. His poetry is distinguished by a Christian mysticism, moving on the verge between dream and reality, the physical and the metaphysical.
Eyvind Johnson and Harry Martinson developed the Swedish autobiographical novel. Johnson wrote the novel series Romanen om Olof (1934–1937), and Martinson published Flowering Nettles in 1935.
Eyvind Johnson took a stand against nazism in his novel trilogy Krilon, written between 1941 and 1943. He also wrote acclaimed historical novels.

In the Seventies, Swedish poets took up the beat tradition from the US as a reaction against the experimental Sixties. A stencil movement grew out of the little magazines, and Bruno K. Öijer emerged from it, developing lyrical performance inspired by Antonin Artaud's "Theatre of cruelty".
Öyvind Fahlström's 1954 concrete poetry manifesto was titled "Hätila ragulpr på fåtskliaben". Other Swedish concrete poets included Åke Hodell, Bengt Emil Johnson and Leif Nylén.

politics.text: The Kingdom of Norway was long held in personal union by Denmark, then fell to Sweden after the Napoleonic Wars. It only attained full independence in 1905.
Finland had been an autonomous grand duchy within the Russian Empire since 1809. It declared independence in 1917, during the Soviet revolution of Russia.

Germany's policy toward Jews was genocidal, and the Danish Jews avoided German persecution only until 1943, when the Germans struck. Denmark was better prepared, and Danes made devoted efforts to protect their Jews. More than 96% of the Jewish population was boated to safety in Sweden, while others found refuge with Christian Danish families and organizations.

Iceland declared its independence from Denmark in 1944, while Denmark was under the occupation of Nazi Germany. British and American armed forces were defending Iceland from Nazi invasion, and they encouraged the declaration.

In 1942, Norwegian police controlled by the Quisling government aided in the capture of Norwegian Jews, as part of cooperation with Germany's genocidal policy. Even so, Norwegians saved over half of the Jewish population from Nazi death camps and helped them escape to safety in Sweden, even though they ran the risk of being severely punished for aiding Jews.

After the war, the Scandinavian countries discussed a defence union that would have acted as a single bloc in foreign policy and security. Norway resigned from the talks when it learned the western alliance could not supply arms. Denmark was still willing, but Sweden saw few advantages and the proposal fell.

After a 1972 referendum, Denmark became the first Scandinavian member of the European Economic Community in 1973. Norway remains outside the European Union after referendums on membership in 1972 and 1994, though it is in the European Economic Area.

After World War II, the Scandinavian countries discussed a defence union that would have acted as a single bloc on security issues. A joint committee debated it in the winter of 1948–1949, but Cold War tension and preparations for the North Atlantic Treaty overshadowed the effort.

With the acquiescence of the Kingdom of Sweden, German troops moved from northern Norway across northern Sweden into Finland, which had become an ally of Nazi Germany. In the spring of 1941, the German and Finnish armies invaded the Soviet Union together.
Finland had a grievance against the Soviet Union because the Red Army had invaded southeastern Finland in the Winter War of 1939 to 1940. The Soviets took a large area of territory away from Finland.
Sweden remained neutral after a heated debate over the Cold War alliances. It eventually joined NATO on 7 March 2024, following the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Denmark voted no to the Maastricht Treaty in 1992, but reversed the decision after negotiating opt-outs. Membership of the Euro was rejected by referendum in both Denmark and Sweden.

philosophy.text: Although Scandinavia adopted Christian ethics, the pillars of Old Norse philosophy are said to remain vital to many Scandinavians. That tradition stresses wisdom, self-reliance and independence. Its most important source is the Hávamál, a poem attributed to Odin and called the "Nicomachean Ethics of the North".

Axel Hägerström taught at Uppsala University from 1893 until his retirement in 1933. He attacked the then dominant philosophical idealism of the followers of Christopher Jacob Boström. He is best known as a founder of the Uppsala school of philosophy, the Swedish counterpart of Anglo-American Analytical Philosophy.

Arne Næss, a Norwegian philosopher, coined the term "deep ecology" and became an important figure in the late twentieth century environmental movement. He combined his ecological vision with Gandhian nonviolence and on several occasions took part in direct action. In 1970, he chained himself to rocks in front of the Mardalsfossen waterfall and refused to come down until plans for a dam were dropped; police carried the demonstrators away, and the dam was built anyway.

Knud Ejler Løgstrup was a Danish philosopher and Lutheran theologian whose work combined phenomenology, ethics and theology. It has had considerable influence in postwar Nordic thought. His 1956 book The Ethical Demand develops an account of a demand he took to be built into our experience of life with other people.

Lee M. Hollander, an American philologist at the University of Texas at Austin, became familiar with the works of Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard while in Oslo. His translation was published in 1923 at the suggestion of Howard Mumford Jones. When Doubleday reprinted it in 1960, he was recognized as a pioneer translator of Kierkegaard into English.

Hägerström rejected metaphysics entirely, and his motto was "Praeterea censeo metaphysicam esse delendam", paraphrasing Cato's famous "delenda Carthago". He regarded value judgements as mere emotional expressions in the form of judgements. Critics called his philosophy "value nihilism", a label invented by journalists.

Hägerström is considered the founding father of the Scandinavian school of legal realism. His disciples Karl Olivecrona, Alf Ross and Anders Vilhelm Lundstedt took a similar view of the language of Western law. Because they rejected natural law, they also rejected the concept of human rights.

Finnish philosopher Georg Henrik von Wright was known for his work in deontic logic and on Wittgenstein's later philosophy, and also for his moral pessimism about the Myth of Progress. He succeeded Wittgenstein as professor at Cambridge in 1948. He was one of three scholars left Wittgenstein's literary estate.

Alf Ross, a Danish legal philosopher, earned his doctorate in philosophy at Uppsala University in 1929 under Axel Hägerström. In 1959 he debated H. L. A. Hart, a debate important in framing the modern conflict between legal positivism and legal realism.

Løgstrup belonged from the 1930s to Tidehverv, a strongly anti-pietist movement within the Danish Church that held a dialectical theology heavily influenced by Kierkegaard. He drifted away from the group and its interpretation of Kierkegaard, and broke with it in the early 1950s.

Arne Næss said that the real motivation to "free nature" was spiritual and intuitive. He argued that supporters of deep ecology came from various religious and spiritual traditions, united in believing that all living creatures have intrinsic value, irrespective of their use to mankind.

In the 21st century, Arne Næss came to be recognized as a pioneer of experimental philosophy, a term he himself used, for his empirical semantics research. One of his early publications in this area was "Truth" as Conceived by Those Who Are Not Professional Philosophers, from 1938.

The Hägerström Lectures at Uppsala University were initiated by Stig Kanger and inaugurated in 1971. Each invited a distinguished philosopher for a week of five open lectures. They were named for Axel Hägerström, founding father of the Uppsala School of ethics and Scandinavian Legal Realism.

culture.text: Christianity was the religion of virtually all Swedes from the 12th to the early 20th century, but it has declined rapidly since. The Church of Sweden's membership fell from 95% in 1972 to 82% in 2000, and it was 50.7% in 2025.

Norse mythology was little known outside Scandinavia until the 19th-century Viking revival. In the later 20th century, references to it became common in science fiction and fantasy literature, role-playing games and even Japanese animation.

The Church of Sweden was the state religion until 2000, and in 1972 some 95% of Swedes belonged to it. By 2000 that share had fallen to 82%, and by 2025 it was 50.7%. Membership has been declining by about 1% each year.

Iceland has seen a rise in people who declare no religious affiliation. Those explicitly unaffiliated with any religion, philosophy or life stance rose from 1.3% in 1990 to 7.67% in 2026. Meanwhile, people following religions or life stances not recognised in the civil registry, combined with a small share of minor religions, rose from 0.6% to about 21% of the population.

The Lutheran Church of Sweden was the state religion until 2000. Until 1996, all newborns with at least one parent in the church were also registered as members, so most Swedes were baptised at birth.

In Iceland, citizens declaring no religious affiliation owe an equivalent church tax to the University of Iceland. The share of Icelanders explicitly unaffiliated with any religion was 7.67% in 2026, up from 1.3% in 1990.

In 2021, Christians made up about 59.6% of Sweden's population, while 37.9% were unaffiliated and 2.5% belonged to other religions. Most Christians belonged to the Church of Sweden, which had 53.2% of the population that year. Christianity had once been the religion of virtually all Swedes.

In the early 2010s the Zuist Church was founded in Iceland, and the state recognised it in 2013. In late 2015 a new board turned it into a protest against the church tax by promising to redistribute the tax funds to members, and about three thousand people joined within weeks.

Muslims are the largest non-Christian religious group in Sweden, followed by Buddhists, Jews and Hindus. Jews are one of Sweden's five official national minorities, and Yiddish is one of its officially recognised minority languages.

In the early 2010s the Zuist Church, a Mesopotamian Neopagan group, was founded in Iceland and recognised by the state in 2013. In late 2015 new leaders turned it into a protest against the church tax, promising to redistribute the tax funds to members. About three thousand people joined within weeks.

The Zuist founders were reinstated as its board in late 2017 and kept the principle of redistributing funds among members, called amargi in Sumerian. In 2019 they were accused of tax fraud, but were acquitted of all charges in the spring of 2022.

In late 2017 the original founders of Iceland's Zuist Church regained its board and kept the principle of redistributing funds among members, called amargi in the Sumerian language. In 2019 they were accused of tax fraud, but they were acquitted of all charges in spring 2022.
